claim: Notch signaling regulates cell survival in mammalian cells.
source: Cell survival is one of several processes regulated by the Notch pathway in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about Notch signaling.

claim: Non-nuclear Notch signaling activates autophagy in murine natural T-regulatory cells.
source: Here we report functional outcomes of non-nuclear Notch signaling to activate autophagy, a conserved cellular response to nutrient stress, regulating survival in murine natural T-regulatory cells (Tregs), an immune subset controlling tolerance and inflammation.
evidence: This is the primary finding reported in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Induction of autophagy in Tregs required ligand-dependent Notch intracellular domain (NIC) activity.
source: Induction of autophagy required ligand-dependent, Notch intracellular domain (NIC) activity, which controlled mitochondrial organization and survival of activated Tregs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using GSI inhibitors and ligand ablation shown in Figure 2.

claim: NIC activity controlled mitochondrial organization in activated Tregs.
source: Induction of autophagy required ligand-dependent, Notch intracellular domain (NIC) activity, which controlled mitochondrial organization and survival of activated Tregs.
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial imaging and FRAP analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: NIC immune-precipitated with Beclin and Atg14, constituents of the autophagy initiation complex.
source: Consistently, NIC immune-precipitated Beclin and Atg14, constituents of the autophagy initiation complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2J and 2K.

claim: Ectopic expression of Atg3 restored autophagy in Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: Further, ectopic expression of an effector of autophagy (Atg3) or recombinant NIC tagged to a nuclear export signal (NIC-NES), restored autophagy and suppressor function in Notch1-/- Tregs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2H and Figure 3J.

claim: Ectopic expression of NIC-NES restored autophagy in Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: Further, ectopic expression of an effector of autophagy (Atg3) or recombinant NIC tagged to a nuclear export signal (NIC-NES), restored autophagy and suppressor function in Notch1-/- Tregs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2I and Figure 3K.

claim: Ectopic expression of Atg3 restored suppressor function in Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: Further, ectopic expression of an effector of autophagy (Atg3) or recombinant NIC tagged to a nuclear export signal (NIC-NES), restored autophagy and suppressor function in Notch1-/- Tregs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Ectopic expression of NIC-NES restored suppressor function in Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: Further, ectopic expression of an effector of autophagy (Atg3) or recombinant NIC tagged to a nuclear export signal (NIC-NES), restored autophagy and suppressor function in Notch1-/- Tregs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5G and Figure 6A.

claim: Notch1 deficiency in the Treg lineage resulted in immune hyperactivity.
source: Furthermore, Notch1 deficiency in the Treg lineage resulted in immune hyperactivity, implicating Notch activity in Treg homeostasis.
evidence: This is shown in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice analysis in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Notch signaling through Notch1 is obligatory for acquisition of T-cell fate.
source: Signaling through Notch1 is obligatory for acquisition of T-cell fate (Radtke et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Notch signaling is differentially activated during T-cell development and in mature T-cells.
source: However, Notch signaling is differentially activated during T-cell development and in mature T-cells, including the differentiation of induced Tregs (iTregs) from Foxp3-ve naive T-cell precursors (Radtke et al., 1999; Laky et al., 2015; Maekawa et al., 2015; Yvon et al., 2003; Wolfer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Foxp3 specifies Treg identity.
source: The transcription factor Foxp3 specifies Treg identity and unlike in induced (i)Tregs where Notch1 regulates Foxp3 expression in response to activation cues, in naturally arising Tregs, Foxp3 expression is developmentally regulated (Fontenot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: In induced Tregs, Notch1 regulates Foxp3 expression in response to activation cues.
source: The transcription factor Foxp3 specifies Treg identity and unlike in induced (i)Tregs where Notch1 regulates Foxp3 expression in response to activation cues, in naturally arising Tregs, Foxp3 expression is developmentally regulated (Fontenot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to naturally arising Tregs and supported by citation.

claim: In naturally arising Tregs, Foxp3 expression is developmentally regulated.
source: The transcription factor Foxp3 specifies Treg identity and unlike in induced (i)Tregs where Notch1 regulates Foxp3 expression in response to activation cues, in naturally arising Tregs, Foxp3 expression is developmentally regulated (Fontenot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Activated Tregs are distinguished by non-nuclear Notch1 signaling.
source: Interestingly, activated Tregs are also distinguished by non-nuclear Notch1 signaling (Perumalsamy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by imaging in Figure 5A.

claim: Macro-autophagy is a conserved catabolic process that buffers cells from limiting nutrient conditions.
source: Macro-autophagy (autophagy) is a conserved catabolic process, which buffers cells from limiting nutrient conditions (Nakatogawa et al., 2009),and is controlled by the evolutionarily conserved Atg/ATG family of proteins (Nakatogawa et al., 2009; Mizushima et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Autophagy is controlled by the evolutionarily conserved Atg/ATG family of proteins.
source: Macro-autophagy (autophagy) is a conserved catabolic process, which buffers cells from limiting nutrient conditions (Nakatogawa et al., 2009),and is controlled by the evolutionarily conserved Atg/ATG family of proteins (Nakatogawa et al., 2009; Mizushima et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Autophagy is implicated in the regulation of diverse aspects of immunity including the differentiation and homeostasis of CD8+ memory T-cells.
source: Autophagy is implicated in the regulation of diverse aspects of immunity including the differentiation and homeostasis of CD8+ memory T-cells and Treg function amongst other cell types (Deretic et al., 2013; Parekh et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Autophagy is implicated in Treg function.
source: Autophagy is implicated in the regulation of diverse aspects of immunity including the differentiation and homeostasis of CD8+ memory T-cells and Treg function amongst other cell types (Deretic et al., 2013; Parekh et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: T-cells depend on cytokines for nutrient uptake and survival.
source: T-cells depend on cytokines for nutrient uptake and survival (Purushothaman and Sarin, 2009; Vella et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Notch1 activity regulates survival in the absence of exogenous cytokines of activated Tregs.
source: A role for Notch1 activity in regulating survival in the absence of exogenous cytokines of activated Tregs has been reported (Perumalsamy et al., 2012), however, the cellular mechanisms activated by Notch1 in this context are not known.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Autophagy is implicated in survival in response to nutrient stressors.
source: Autophagy, a conserved catabolic process is implicated in survival in response to nutrient stressors (Lum et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Cytokine withdrawal triggers an increase in the LC3II isoform in Tregs after 6 hours.
source: An increase in the LC3II isoform was detected in lysates of Tregs, which had been cultured without IL-2 for 6 hr, relative to the onset of the assay (T0) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LC3 staining changes from diffuse to large puncta following cytokine withdrawal in Tregs.
source: Immunostaining with the same antibody as used for the immunoblots and visualization of intact cells by confocal microscopy, showed that diffuse LC3 staining observed in Tregs at T0, progressively changed to large, readily visualized puncta by 6 hr, persisting till 15 hr following cytokine-withdrawal (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1B.

claim: Quantifiable changes in fluorescence intensity and size of LC3 puncta were detected over 15 hours following cytokine withdrawal.
source: Quantifiable changes in fluorescence intensity and size of puncta were detected over this period (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification plots in Figure 1B and supplementary figure.

claim: Tregs are viable throughout the 15-hour cytokine withdrawal assay.
source: It should be noted that Tregs are viable throughout the course of this assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by viability data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Atg5 protein increased in Tregs following cytokine withdrawal.
source: The protein Atg5, a molecular indicator of the activation of autophagy (Mizushima, et al., 2011), was also increased following cytokine withdrawal as detected by Immunoblots of Tregs cultured without cytokine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 1C.

claim: Bafilomycin A blocks autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: The inclusion of Bafilomycin A (Baf), which blocks autophagosome-lysosome fusion or 3-Methyladenine (3MA), at the onset of the cytokine deprivation assay resulted in cell death, when measured at 15 hr, indicating that Treg survival was abrogated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of Bafilomycin A.

claim: Bafilomycin A treatment resulted in Treg cell death following cytokine withdrawal.
source: The inclusion of Bafilomycin A (Baf), which blocks autophagosome-lysosome fusion or 3-Methyladenine (3MA), at the onset of the cytokine deprivation assay resulted in cell death, when measured at 15 hr, indicating that Treg survival was abrogated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 1D.

claim: 3-Methyladenine treatment resulted in Treg cell death following cytokine withdrawal.
source: The inclusion of Bafilomycin A (Baf), which blocks autophagosome-lysosome fusion or 3-Methyladenine (3MA), at the onset of the cytokine deprivation assay resulted in cell death, when measured at 15 hr, indicating that Treg survival was abrogated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 1D.

claim: Loss of Vps34 in activated Tregs resulted in cell death following cytokine withdrawal.
source: The loss of either VpS34 or Atg7 in activated Tregs resulted in cell death following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 1E,F), establishing a requirement for these intermediates in Treg survival.
evidence: This is demonstrated by shRNA knockdown experiments in Figure 1E.

claim: Loss of Atg7 in activated Tregs resulted in cell death following cytokine withdrawal.
source: The loss of either VpS34 or Atg7 in activated Tregs resulted in cell death following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 1E,F), establishing a requirement for these intermediates in Treg survival.
evidence: This is demonstrated by shRNA knockdown experiments in Figure 1F.

claim: Vps34 is required for Treg survival following cytokine withdrawal.
source: The loss of either VpS34 or Atg7 in activated Tregs resulted in cell death following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 1E,F), establishing a requirement for these intermediates in Treg survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell death observed upon Vps34 knockdown.

claim: Atg7 is required for Treg survival following cytokine withdrawal.
source: The loss of either VpS34 or Atg7 in activated Tregs resulted in cell death following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 1E,F), establishing a requirement for these intermediates in Treg survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell death observed upon Atg7 knockdown.

claim: GSI-X inhibits γ-secretase enzyme activity.
source: A pharmacological inhibitor of the enzyme γ-secretase, (GS inhibitor)-X, inhibits cleavage (S3 cleavage post ligand binding) and release of NIC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of GSI-X.

claim: GSI-X inhibits cleavage and release of NIC.
source: A pharmacological inhibitor of the enzyme γ-secretase, (GS inhibitor)-X, inhibits cleavage (S3 cleavage post ligand binding) and release of NIC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of GSI-X.

claim: Culturing Tregs with GSI-X abrogated survival following cytokine withdrawal.
source: Culturing Tregs with GSI-X abrogated survival following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 2A.

claim: In GSI treated cells, Notch1 staining was restricted to the cell membrane.
source: In GSI treated cells, immunestaining for Notch1 showed that that staining was restricted to the cell membrane, confirming that receptor cleavage is disrupted (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 2B.

claim: Induction of LC3 puncta was not observed in Tregs cultured with GSI during cytokine withdrawal.
source: Further, induction of LC3 puncta was not observed in Tregs cultured with GSI during cytokine withdrawal (Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that autophagy is not activated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC3 staining in Figure 2C.

claim: Delta Like Ligand (DLL)-1 has a non-redundant role in Treg survival.
source: Earlier work from the laboratory had identified a non-redundant role for the ligand Delta Like Ligand (DLL)-1 in Treg survival.
evidence: This refers to previous work from the same laboratory.

claim: Ablation of DLL-1 in Tregs compromised survival following cytokine withdrawal.
source: Confirming ligand-dependence, ablation of DLL-1 in Tregs, compromised survival and induction of LC3 puncta in cells cultured without cytokine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by shRNA knockdown experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ablation of DLL-1 in Tregs compromised induction of LC3 puncta in cells cultured without cytokine.
source: Confirming ligand-dependence, ablation of DLL-1 in Tregs, compromised survival and induction of LC3 puncta in cells cultured without cytokine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC3 staining in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Induction of LC3 puncta in Tregs was unchanged following shRNA-mediated ablation of RBPJ-κ.
source: Contrastingly, but in agreement with published analysis of NIC1 signaling in Tregs, both the induction of LC3 puncta or cytokine-independent survival in Tregs was unchanged following shRNA-mediated ablation of RBPJ-κ, a co-factor of NIC transcription (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC3 staining in Figure 2D.

claim: Cytokine-independent survival in Tregs was unchanged following shRNA-mediated ablation of RBPJ-κ.
source: Contrastingly, but in agreement with published analysis of NIC1 signaling in Tregs, both the induction of LC3 puncta or cytokine-independent survival in Tregs was unchanged following shRNA-mediated ablation of RBPJ-κ, a co-factor of NIC transcription (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DiOC6 uptake data in Figure 2E.

claim: RBPJ-κ is a co-factor of NIC transcription.
source: Contrastingly, but in agreement with published analysis of NIC1 signaling in Tregs, both the induction of LC3 puncta or cytokine-independent survival in Tregs was unchanged following shRNA-mediated ablation of RBPJ-κ, a co-factor of NIC transcription (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBPJ-κ function.

claim: Ablation of RBPJ-κ attenuated expression of Hes1.
source: The ablation of RBPJ-κ attenuated expression of Hes1 a target of NIC (Figure 2F) confirming efficacy of shRNA ablation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot in Figure 2F.

claim: Hes1 is a target of NIC.
source: The ablation of RBPJ-κ attenuated expression of Hes1 a target of NIC (Figure 2F) confirming efficacy of shRNA ablation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch signaling.

claim: Ligand dependent Notch1 activity is required for autophagy in Tregs.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that ligand dependent Notch1 activity was required for autophagy and regulation was independent of canonical Notch interactions, such as those requiring RBPJ-κ (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the GSI and DLL-1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Notch1 regulation of autophagy is independent of canonical Notch interactions requiring RBPJ-κ.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that ligand dependent Notch1 activity was required for autophagy and regulation was independent of canonical Notch interactions, such as those requiring RBPJ-κ (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the RBPJ-κ knockdown experiments showing no effect on autophagy.

claim: The induction of LC3 puncta in response to cytokine withdrawal was blunted in Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: The induction of LC3 puncta in response to cytokine withdrawal was blunted in Notch1-/- Tregs (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), and cell survival compromised in cells cultured without cytokine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC3 staining in Figure 2G.

claim: Cell survival was compromised in Notch1-/- Tregs cultured without cytokine.
source: The induction of LC3 puncta in response to cytokine withdrawal was blunted in Notch1-/- Tregs (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), and cell survival compromised in cells cultured without cytokine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Retroviral transduction of recombinant Atg3 in Notch1-/- Tregs restored survival following cytokine withdrawal.
source: In consonance with dependence on autophagy, retroviral transduction of recombinant Atg3 in Notch1-/- Tregs restored survival following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 2H.

claim: Atg3 is an E2-ubiquitin-like-conjugating enzyme that catalyzes the lipidation of LC3I.
source: Atg3 is an E2-ubiquitin-like-conjugating enzyme, which catalyzes the lipidation of the effector protein LC3I (ATG8) (Mizushma et al., 1998), a key step in autophagy progression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Lipidation of LC3I is a key step in autophagy progression.
source: Atg3 is an E2-ubiquitin-like-conjugating enzyme, which catalyzes the lipidation of the effector protein LC3I (ATG8) (Mizushma et al., 1998), a key step in autophagy progression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Atg3 is implicated in maintaining mitochondrial health under conditions of nutrient stress.
source: Atg3 is also implicated in maintaining mitochondrial health under conditions of nutrient stress (Besteiro et al., 2011; Radoshevich and Debnath, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Notch1 activation of autophagy is necessary for Treg survival following cytokine withdrawal in culture.
source: From these experiments we concluded that Notch1 activation of autophagy was necessary for Treg survival following cytokine withdrawal in culture.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments showing Notch1 dependence of autophagy and survival.

claim: NIC is enriched in the cytoplasm of Tregs.
source: NIC is enriched in the cytoplasm of Tregs (shown later and Perumalsamy et al., 2012), and we tested if non-nuclear NIC activity regulated autophagy following cytokine withdrawal.
evidence: This is supported by citation and imaging data shown later in Figure 5A.

claim: NIC-NES expression protected Notch1-/- Tregs from apoptosis following cytokine-withdrawal.
source: NIC-NES expression protected Notch1-/- Tregs from apoptosis following cytokine-withdrawal (Figure 2I) and this protection is attenuated by the inclusion of Baf or 3MA (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 2I.

claim: Protection from apoptosis by NIC-NES is attenuated by Bafilomycin or 3MA.
source: NIC-NES expression protected Notch1-/- Tregs from apoptosis following cytokine-withdrawal (Figure 2I) and this protection is attenuated by the inclusion of Baf or 3MA (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 2I.

claim: Non-nuclear NIC activity can activate autophagy signaling in Tregs following cytokine withdrawal.
source: Thus, non-nuclear NIC activity could activate autophagy signaling in Tregs following cytokine withdrawal.
evidence: This is inferred from the NIC-NES rescue experiments.

claim: An antibody specific for Notch1 immune-precipitated Beclin1 and Atg14 but not Vps34 and LC3 in Tregs undergoing cytokine-deprivation.
source: In Tregs initiated into cytokine-deprivation, an antibody specific for Notch1 (mN1A) but not an IgG (isotype control) immune-precipitated Beclin1 and Atg14 but not Vps34 and LC3 (Figure 2J), indicating that NIC formed complexes with specific components of the autophagy pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 2J.

claim: NIC forms complexes with specific components of the autophagy pathway.
source: In Tregs initiated into cytokine-deprivation, an antibody specific for Notch1 (mN1A) but not an IgG (isotype control) immune-precipitated Beclin1 and Atg14 but not Vps34 and LC3 (Figure 2J), indicating that NIC formed complexes with specific components of the autophagy pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Beclin1 immune-precipitated NIC.
source: In the reverse analysis, Beclin1 immune-precipitated NIC confirming the specificity of its association with NIC and this complex also included Atg14 and Vps34 (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 2K.

claim: The Beclin1-NIC complex includes Atg14 and Vps34.
source: In the reverse analysis, Beclin1 immune-precipitated NIC confirming the specificity of its association with NIC and this complex also included Atg14 and Vps34 (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 2K.

claim: Beclin is detected in complexes that include either Vps34 or NIC with both complexes including Atg14.
source: Thus, Beclin is detected in complexes that include either Vps34 or NIC with both complexes including Atg14 as expected.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figures 2J and 2K.

claim: Vps34 and Beclin form multiple and dynamic cellular complexes.
source: Vps34 and Beclin are known to form multiple and dynamic cellular complexes, which are regulated by the phosphorylation of the proteins themselves as well their interacting partners (Kang et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Vps34-Beclin complexes are regulated by phosphorylation of the proteins and their interacting partners.
source: Vps34 and Beclin are known to form multiple and dynamic cellular complexes, which are regulated by the phosphorylation of the proteins themselves as well their interacting partners (Kang et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: NIC forms complexes with proteins regulating autophagy in Tregs.
source: That NIC formed complexes with proteins regulating autophagy in Tregs, indicated a more direct role for Notch1 in the autophagic cascade, although the molecular regulation and dynamics of this interaction remains to be dissected.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Mitochondrial re-modeling and activity control cellular responses to changing bioenergetic needs.
source: Mitochondrial re-modeling and activity control cellular responses to changing bioenergetic needs, which facilitate transitions between nutrient-replete and deficient conditions (Rambold et al., 2011, Hailey et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Notch modulation of mitochondrial function has been suggested in earlier work.
source: Since Notch modulation of mitochondrial function has been suggested in earlier work (Perumalsamy et al., 2010; Kasahara et al., 2013), mitochondrial organization and integrity in Tregs were next examined.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Activated Tregs undergo almost no change in mitochondrial transmembrane potential following cytokine withdrawal.
source: Activated Tregs undergo almost no change in MTP following cytokine withdrawal, consistent with their survival (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DiOC6 uptake data in Figure 3A.

claim: Inclusion of GSI compromised mitochondrial function in Tregs within 8-9 hours of culture.
source: However, inclusion of GSI compromised mitochondrial function as it triggered a loss of MTP within 8–9 hr of culture (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DiOC6 uptake data in Figure 3A.

claim: Mitochondrial activity is regulated by Notch in Tregs.
source: Thus, mitochondrial activity was regulated by Notch in Tregs.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSI experiments showing loss of MTP.

claim: In live activated Tregs, mitochondria appear as interconnected structures.
source: In live activated Tregs, mitochondria marked with MitoTracker Green and visualized by confocal microscopy appear as interconnected structures, which remained so following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: Mitochondria in activated Tregs remain interconnected following cytokine withdrawal.
source: In live activated Tregs, mitochondria marked with MitoTracker Green and visualized by confocal microscopy appear as interconnected structures, which remained so following cytokine withdrawal (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: shRNA-mediated ablation of DLL-1 disrupted mitochondrial organization in Tregs cultured without cytokine.
source: Mitochondrial organization in cells cultured without cytokine was disrupted by perturbations of Notch activity, which included shRNA-mediated ablation of the Notch ligand DLL-1 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or shRNA mediated ablation of Notch1 (Figure 3D) or by the inclusion of GSI-X (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1Cii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3C.

claim: shRNA-mediated ablation of Notch1 disrupted mitochondrial organization in Tregs cultured without cytokine.
source: Mitochondrial organization in cells cultured without cytokine was disrupted by perturbations of Notch activity, which included shRNA-mediated ablation of the Notch ligand DLL-1 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or shRNA mediated ablation of Notch1 (Figure 3D) or by the inclusion of GSI-X (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1Cii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3D.

claim: Inclusion of GSI-X disrupted mitochondrial organization in Tregs cultured without cytokine.
source: Mitochondrial organization in cells cultured without cytokine was disrupted by perturbations of Notch activity, which included shRNA-mediated ablation of the Notch ligand DLL-1 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or shRNA mediated ablation of Notch1 (Figure 3D) or by the inclusion of GSI-X (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1Cii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3E.

claim: Addition of Bafilomycin disrupted mitochondrial organization in Tregs cultured without cytokine.
source: Mitochondrial organization was also disrupted by the addition of Baf (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ciii) or by shRNA-mediated ablation of Atg7 (Figure 3G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C iv,v), implicating autophagic signaling in organelle integrity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3F.

claim: shRNA-mediated ablation of Atg7 disrupted mitochondrial organization in Tregs cultured without cytokine.
source: Mitochondrial organization was also disrupted by the addition of Baf (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ciii) or by shRNA-mediated ablation of Atg7 (Figure 3G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C iv,v), implicating autophagic signaling in organelle integrity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3G.

claim: Autophagic signaling is implicated in mitochondrial organelle integrity.
source: Mitochondrial organization was also disrupted by the addition of Baf (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ciii) or by shRNA-mediated ablation of Atg7 (Figure 3G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C iv,v), implicating autophagic signaling in organelle integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the disruption of mitochondria upon autophagy inhibition.

claim: Uptake of DiOC6 was significantly lower in Notch1-/- Tregs relative to WT Tregs cultured in IL-2.
source: Uptake of DiOC6 was significantly lower in Notch1-/- Tregs relative to WT Tregs cultured in IL-2 (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DiOC6 uptake data in Figure 3H.

claim: Following cytokine withdrawal, further loss of mitochondrial transmembrane potential indicated compromised mitochondrial function in Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: Following cytokine withdrawal, further loss of MTP, indicated compromised mitochondrial function in Notch1-/- Tregs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DiOC6 uptake data in Figure 3H.

claim: Fluorescence recovery in WT Tregs was high in FRAP analysis, consistent with a connected mitochondrial morphology.
source: Fluorescence recovery in WT Tregs was high, which is consistent with a connected morphology of the organelle (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP analysis in Figure 3I.

claim: Low FRAP in Notch1-/- Tregs is indicative of discontinuous mitochondrial structures.
source: Low FRAP in Notch1-/- Tregs is indicative of discontinuous structures (Figure 3I), which was confirmed by microscopy (Figure 3I inset and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP analysis and imaging in Figure 3I.

claim: The punctate morphology of mitochondria in Notch1-/- Tregs was reduced in cells expressing recombinant Atg3.
source: The punctate morphology of mitochondria in Notch1-/- Tregs was reduced, with the organelle appearing more tubular and connected in cells expressing recombinant Atg3 (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) or recombinant NIC-NES (Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) relative to cells expressing an empty vector control (Figure 3J,K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3J.

claim: The punctate morphology of mitochondria in Notch1-/- Tregs was reduced in cells expressing recombinant NIC-NES.
source: The punctate morphology of mitochondria in Notch1-/- Tregs was reduced, with the organelle appearing more tubular and connected in cells expressing recombinant Atg3 (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) or recombinant NIC-NES (Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) relative to cells expressing an empty vector control (Figure 3J,K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MitoTracker imaging in Figure 3K.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial transmembrane potential and mitochondrial fragmentation is associated with poor survival outcomes following cytokine withdrawal in Tregs.
source: Thus a loss of MTP and mitochondrial fragmentation was associated with poor survival outcomes following cytokine withdrawal in Tregs.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death.

claim: NIC is critical for the integrity and function of mitochondria in Tregs.
source: Our experiments established that NIC and autophagy signaling were critical for the integrity and function of mitochondria in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with NIC-NES.

claim: Autophagy signaling is critical for the integrity and function of mitochondria in Tregs.
source: Our experiments established that NIC and autophagy signaling were critical for the integrity and function of mitochondria in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with Atg3.

claim: T-effectors do not survive cytokine withdrawal.
source: For this, we employed T-effectors generated from naïve T-cell precursors, as T-effectors do not survive cytokine withdrawal (Purushothaman and Sarin, 2009) and we had prior evidence that ectopic expression of recombinant NIC protected T-effectors from apoptosis in this context (Bheeshmachar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Ectopic expression of recombinant NIC protected T-effectors from apoptosis following cytokine withdrawal.
source: For this, we employed T-effectors generated from naïve T-cell precursors, as T-effectors do not survive cytokine withdrawal (Purushothaman and Sarin, 2009) and we had prior evidence that ectopic expression of recombinant NIC protected T-effectors from apoptosis in this context (Bheeshmachar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: T-effectors do not increase LC3 puncta following cytokine deprivation.
source: T-effectors - generated as described in methods by TCR stimulation of naïve T-cells - do not increase LC3 puncta or the LC3II isoform following cytokine deprivation (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC3 staining and immunoblot in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: T-effectors do not increase the LC3II isoform following cytokine deprivation.
source: T-effectors - generated as described in methods by TCR stimulation of naïve T-cells - do not increase LC3 puncta or the LC3II isoform following cytokine deprivation (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot in Figure 4B.

claim: Endogenous NIC is nuclear localized in T-effectors.
source: Endogenous NIC is nuclear localized in T-effectors unlike Tregs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ectopic expression of NIC-NES protected T-effectors from apoptosis triggered by cytokine withdrawal.
source: As was seen with Tregs, the ectopic expression of NIC-NES protected T-effectors from apoptosis triggered by cytokine withdrawal (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 4C.

claim: NIC-NLS did not confer protection from cell death in T-effectors following cytokine withdrawal.
source: However a recombinant NIC modified by the inclusion of a Nuclear Localization Signal (NIC-NLS, Figure 4C inset), which enforces localization to the nucleus did not confer protection from cell death (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 4C.

claim: The protective effect of NIC-NES was reproduced in T-effectors derived from Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox naïve T-cells.
source: We ruled out a role for endogenous Notch1 in this context, by reproducing the protective effect of NIC-NES in T-effectors derived from Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox naïve T-cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 4D.

claim: Protection from cell death by NIC-NES in T-effectors was abrogated by inclusion of Bafilomycin or 3MA.
source: Further, protection from cell death was abrogated if inhibitors of autophagy - Baf or 3MA - were included in culture (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis data in Figure 4D.

claim: Mitochondria in T-effectors do not demonstrate contiguity in FRAP assays.
source: Notably, mitochondria in T-effectors do not demonstrate contiguity in FRAP assays (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) or by confocal image analysis (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: The crosstalk between Notch1 and autophagy for the regulation of survival is not restricted to Tregs alone.
source: Thus, the analysis indicated that the crosstalk between Notch1 and autophagy for the regulation of survival is not restricted to Tregs alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the T-effector experiments showing NIC-NES protection.

claim: Foxp3 expression was comparable in activated Tregs generated from Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice and matched genetic controls.
source: However, Foxp3 expression was comparable in activated Tregs generated from Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice and the matched genetic controls, including Tregs from C57Bl/6 (wildtype) mice (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Foxp3 immunostaining in Figure 5B.

claim: Naïve Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox T-cells cannot be differentiated to express Foxp3 in iTreg polarizing conditions.
source: We recapitulated Notch1-dependence in activation-induced expression of Foxp3 in induced Tregs. Thus, in culture conditions that polarize to the generation of iTregs, in contrast to the genetic control (Cre negative) littermates, naïve Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox T-cells, cannot be differentiated to express Foxp3, (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A upper panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Foxp3 staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Activated Tregs from Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox and genetic control mice showed no striking differences in gene expression of molecules enriched in Treg subsets.
source: In this analysis, activated Tregs of the two genotypes showed no striking differences, with loss of Notch1 transcript serving as the positive (internal) control (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Comparison of gene sets enriched for cytokines associated with Tregs revealed no differences in Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox or genetic control mice.
source: Similarly, comparison of gene sets enriched for cytokines associated with Tregs revealed no differences in the Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox or genetic (Cre negative) control mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gene expression analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The distribution of naïve and memory T-cell subsets in circulation was comparable in Tregs derived from Cre negative controls and Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice.
source: The distribution of naïve and memory T-cell subsets in circulation, an indication of the resting vs. activated state of the immune system was comparable in Tregs derived from Cre negative controls and Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Activated Tregs of wildtype and Notch1-/- genotypes were comparable in in vitro suppressor assays.
source: Indeed, in earlier work when tested for suppressor activity in vitro, activated Tregs of the two genotypes were comparable (Perumalsamy et al 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Tregs transfected with Notch1 shRNA showed attenuated suppressor activity in vivo.
source: On the other hand, in cells isolated from mice injected with Tregs transduced with Notch1 shRNA, OT-II T-cells proliferated robustly (Figure 5E panel iii), and were comparable to proliferation in OT-II cells injected without Tregs (Figure 5E, panel i).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assay in Figure 5E.

claim: Notch1 controls the suppressor activity of Tregs.
source: This indicates that Notch1 controls the suppressor activity of Tregs.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of suppressor activity upon Notch1 knockdown.

claim: Suppressor activity was attenuated in Notch1-/- Tregs compared to wildtype Tregs.
source: Similarly, suppressor activity was attenuated in Notch1-/- Tregs (Figure 5F, compare panels, i and iii) as compared to wildtype Tregs (TregsWT) (Figure 5F panel ii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assay in Figure 5F.

claim: Reconstitution with recombinant NIC restored suppressor activity of Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: However, reconstitution with recombinant NIC restored suppressor activity of Notch1-/- Tregs (Figure 5G, compare iii and ii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assay in Figure 5G.

claim: shRNA to Vps34 abrogated wildtype Treg suppressor activity in vivo.
source: In agreement with the reported requirement of autophagy in Treg function (Parekh et al., 2013, Wei et al., 2016), shRNA to Vps34 abrogated TregsWT suppressor activity relative to the cells treated with the scrambled shRNA (Figure 5H compare iii with ii) as compared to the control group injected without Tregs (Figure 5Hi).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assay in Figure 5H.

claim: Ablation of Vps34 did not modulate the expression of Foxp3.
source: The ablation of Vps34 (inhibition of autophagy) did not modulate the expression of Foxp3 (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Foxp3 staining in Figure 5I.

claim: Ablation of VpS34 in activated Tregs abrogated suppressor activity in vitro.
source: However, in an in vitro assay of Treg function, which measures suppression of conventional T-cell proliferation via stimulation of T-cell receptor in the presence of antigen presenting cells, the ablation of VpS34 in activated Tregs abrogated suppressor activity (Figure 5K, compare i and ii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro suppression assay in Figure 5K.

claim: Vps34 is critical for Treg function.
source: Thus, Vps34 was critical for Treg function and its requirement revealed in suppressor assays performed in vitro or in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of suppressor activity upon Vps34 knockdown.

claim: Suppressor activity was restored in Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with recombinant Atg3 in vivo.
source: Furthermore, suppressor activity in assays in vivo was restored in Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with recombinant Atg3 (Figure 5L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assay in Figure 5L.

claim: Expression of recombinant NIC-NES restored suppressor activity in transferred Notch1-/- Tregs.
source: In the OT-II T-cell proliferation assay, expression of recombinant NIC-NES restored suppressor activity in transferred Notch1-/- Tregs (Figure 6Aii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assay in Figure 6A.

claim: Suppressor activity was not restored in Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with NIC-NLS.
source: Suppressor activity was not restored in Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with NIC-NLS (Figure 6Aiii).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assay in Figure 6A.

claim: Impaired glucose clearance is a feature of obesity.
source: The assay tracks the clearance of glucose injected into the blood stream of obese mice, and builds on the observation that impaired glucose clearance (also referred to as glucose intolerance) is a feature of obesity (Winer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Injection of Tregs corrects defects in glucose clearance in obese mice.
source: In this context, the injection of Tregs has been shown to correct defects in the clearance of glucose, although protection is short-term and persists for 10–15 days (Cipolletta et al., 2012, Feuerer et al.,2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Protection of glucose clearance by Tregs is short-term and persists for 10-15 days.
source: In this context, the injection of Tregs has been shown to correct defects in the clearance of glucose, although protection is short-term and persists for 10–15 days (Cipolletta et al., 2012, Feuerer et al.,2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: There are no deficiencies in Treg number or function reported in obese leptin receptor-deficient mice.
source: The underlying mechanism of correction by Tregs is not understood, as there are no deficiencies in Treg number or function reported in obese (leptin receptor-deficient, Leprdb/db) mice (De Rosa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Clearance of injected glucose from blood in fasting Leprdb/db mice is substantially delayed compared to heterozygous littermates.
source: In agreement with published observations we show that the clearance of (injected) glucose from blood in fasting Leprdb/db mice, is substantially delayed compared to heterozygous (Leprdb/+) littermates (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IPGTT data in Figure 6B.

claim: In Leprdb/db mice injected with wildtype Tregs, clearance of blood glucose is comparable to Leprdb/+ animals.
source: However, in Leprdb/db mice injected with TregsWT, and tested 7–8 days later, clearance of blood glucose is comparable to Leprdb/+animals (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IPGTT data in Figure 6B.

claim: Correction of glucose clearance by Tregs is transient and is lost within 2 weeks following adoptive transfer.
source: Correction is transient and is lost within 2 weeks following adoptive transfer (not shown).
evidence: This is stated but data not shown.

claim: Activated Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with control vector did not improve glucose clearance in obese mice.
source: Hence, we next tested Notch1-/- Tregs in this assay system. Activated Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with the control vector did not improve glucose clearance, however, transferring NIC-NES expressing Notch1-/- Tregs, restored the clearance of glucose to rates comparable to Leprdb/+ mice (Figure 6C), indicating that enrichment of non-nuclear Notch activity restored Notch1-/- Tregs activity in this assay.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IPGTT data in Figure 6C.

claim: Transferring NIC-NES expressing Notch1-/- Tregs restored glucose clearance to rates comparable to Leprdb/+ mice.
source: Hence, we next tested Notch1-/- Tregs in this assay system. Activated Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with the control vector did not improve glucose clearance, however, transferring NIC-NES expressing Notch1-/- Tregs, restored the clearance of glucose to rates comparable to Leprdb/+ mice (Figure 6C), indicating that enrichment of non-nuclear Notch activity restored Notch1-/- Tregs activity in this assay.
evidence: This is demonstrated by IPGTT data in Figure 6C.

claim: Injecting Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with recombinant Atg3 corrected the rate of glucose clearance to a level comparable to control non-obese mice.
source: Similarly, as seen in the T-cell proliferation assay, injecting Notch1-/- Tregs transfected with recombinant Atg3, also corrected the rate of glucose clearance to a level comparable to that of control, non-obese mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by IPGTT data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice were born in reduced numbers (1:16 as against the expected 1:8 ratio).
source: Mice with a Notch1 ablation, were born in reduced numbers (1:16 as against the expected 1:8 ratio), presented with features consistent with dysregulated immune function and some similarities with Scurfy mice, which lack Tregs because of a loss-of-function mutation in the Foxp3 gene (Fontenot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an observation from breeding experiments.

claim: Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice presented with features consistent with dysregulated immune function.
source: Mice with a Notch1 ablation, were born in reduced numbers (1:16 as against the expected 1:8 ratio), presented with features consistent with dysregulated immune function and some similarities with Scurfy mice, which lack Tregs because of a loss-of-function mutation in the Foxp3 gene (Fontenot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an observation from phenotypic analysis of the mice.

claim: Scurfy mice lack Tregs because of a loss-of-function mutation in the Foxp3 gene.
source: Mice with a Notch1 ablation, were born in reduced numbers (1:16 as against the expected 1:8 ratio), presented with features consistent with dysregulated immune function and some similarities with Scurfy mice, which lack Tregs because of a loss-of-function mutation in the Foxp3 gene (Fontenot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice presented with enlarged lymph nodes and increased cellularity relative to Cre-negative littermate controls.
source: Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice (analyzed from 4–8 weeks of age) were viable, presented with enlarged lymph nodes and increased cellularity relative to Cre-negative littermate controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lymph node analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: Increased cellularity in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice resulted from increased numbers of CD4+CD62LlowCD44high (effector memory) and CD4+CD62LhighCD44high (central memory) T-cell subsets.
source: Increased cellularity resulted from increased numbers of CD4+CD62LlowCD44high (effector memory) and CD4+CD62LhighCD44high (central memory) T-cell subsets (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: In Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice injected with WT Tregs, lymph node inflammation was substantially reduced.
source: Further, in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice, which had been injected with WT Tregs, seven days prior to analysis, lymph node inflammation and the number of activated CD4+ T-cell subsets in lymph nodes was substantially reduced (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6F.

claim: In Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice injected with WT Tregs, the number of activated CD4+ T-cell subsets in lymph nodes was substantially reduced.
source: Further, in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice, which had been injected with WT Tregs, seven days prior to analysis, lymph node inflammation and the number of activated CD4+ T-cell subsets in lymph nodes was substantially reduced (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6F.

claim: Defects in Treg function contribute to inflammation in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice.
source: This suggested that defects in Treg function might contribute to the observed inflammation in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of inflammation by WT Treg transfer.

claim: Foxp3 expression was comparable in Tregs from mice of different genotypes.
source: Nonetheless, Foxp3 expression, assessed by immunostaining in Tregs was comparable in mice of the different genotypes (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Foxp3 immunostaining in Figure 6G.

claim: Notch1 plays an important role in immune homeostasis.
source: The analysis of Notch1-/- Tregs in functional assays of inflammation together with the phenotypes of mice with a deletion of Notch1 in Tregs suggests an important role for the receptor in immune homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional assays and mouse phenotypes.

claim: Notch1 regulated autophagy is an integral controlling element of activated Treg homeostasis.
source: In this study we position Notch1 regulated autophagy as an integral controlling element of activated Treg homeostasis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: Survival and function are compromised following perturbations of Notch signaling in wildtype Tregs.
source: This is inferred from the observations that survival and function are compromised following perturbations of Notch signaling or autophagy in TregsWT and the restoration of autophagy and suppressor activity following reconstitution of Notch1-/- Tregs with the nuclear-excluded recombinant NIC-NES or Atg3.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSI and shRNA experiments.

claim: Survival and function are compromised following perturbations of autophagy in wildtype Tregs.
source: This is inferred from the observations that survival and function are compromised following perturbations of Notch signaling or autophagy in TregsWT and the restoration of autophagy and suppressor activity following reconstitution of Notch1-/- Tregs with the nuclear-excluded recombinant NIC-NES or Atg3.
evidence: This is inferred from the Baf, 3MA, and shRNA experiments.

claim: The requirement for Notch1 in thymus-derived activated Tregs is distinct from identified roles for Notch-TGFβ interactions in iTregs.
source: Of note, the requirement for Notch1 in thymus-derived activated Tregs is distinct from identified roles for Notch-TGFβ interactions in iTregs (Samon et al., 2008; Mota et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Notch-induced autophagy is a mechanism of quality control of mitochondrial architecture.
source: More generally, our experiments suggest that Notch-induced autophagy is a mechanism of quality control of mitochondrial architecture.
evidence: This is inferred from the mitochondrial organization experiments.

claim: Cell survival in complex and changing environments associated with inflammation is an important component determining immune cell function.
source: Cell survival in complex and changing environments associated with inflammation is an important component determining immune cell function.
evidence: This is a general statement based on biological knowledge.

claim: The loss of suppressor activity in Notch1-/- Tregs in vivo did not agree with outcomes of suppressor assays in vitro.
source: The loss of suppressor activity in Notch1-/- Tregs in vivo, did not agree with outcomes of suppressor assays in vitro, wherein Notch1 appeared to be dispensable for Treg suppression (Perumalsamy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison between current findings and previous work.

claim: Notch1-/- Tregs suppress T-cell proliferation in vitro because concentrations of cytokines and growth factors build up in the dish.
source: Based on the understanding of Notch activity in Tregs we speculate that Notch1-/- Tregs suppress T-cell proliferation in vitro as concentrations of cytokines and growth factors that build up in the dish likely protect Notch1-/- Tregs from death.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Autophagy controls Treg survival and plays a defining role in maintenance of functional identity.
source: That the ablation of Vps34 compromised Treg activity in both in vivo and in vitro assays, is consistent with autophagy controlling Treg survival and playing a defining role in maintenance of functional identity (Wei et al., 2016), i.e. regulating Foxp3 expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and the Vps34 experiments.

claim: The dynamic regulation of Notch and its role as a critical determinant of Treg differentiation, function and homeostasis has emerged from work by another group.
source: The dynamic regulation of Notch and its role as a critical determinant of Treg differentiation, function and homeostasis has emerged from work by another group (Charbonnier et al.,2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: A recent report defined a critical role for autophagy during differentiation of Tregs.
source: Similarly, a more recent report (Wei et al., 2016), focused on events at the earlier stages of Treg undergoing activation to define a critical role for autophagy during differentiation of Tregs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Deletion of Notch1 in the Treg lineage resulted in features of immune-inflammation consistent with a role for Notch1 in Treg function.
source: Unlike the study by Charbonnier et al., which positions RBPJ-k dependent Notch signaling as a negative regulator of Treg function we find that deletion of Notch1 in the Treg lineage resulted in features of immune-inflammation consistent with a role for Notch1 in Treg function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mouse phenotype.

claim: Both this study and Charbonnier et al. implicate non-canonical Notch1 activity as necessary for maintenance of Treg identity.
source: However, both the studies implicate non-canonical Notch1 activity as necessary for maintenance of Treg identity.
evidence: This is a comparison with published work.

claim: The increased representation of recently activated and T-memory subsets in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice is likely a response to antigens experienced in high barrier housing conditions.
source: We speculate that the increased representation of recently activated and T-memory subsets in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice, observed in our experiments, is likely a response to antigens experienced in the high barrier – but not SPF1 – conditions, that mice are housed in.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The phenotypes of autoimmunity reported in Atg7 deficient mice align with lymphoid proliferation and increased cellularity observed in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice.
source: Interestingly, the phenotypes of autoimmunity reported in Atg7 deficient mice (Wei et al., 2016), align with lymphoid proliferation and increased cellularity we observe in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/loxmice.
evidence: This is a comparison with published work.

claim: The interaction between Notch and autophagy revealed in these experiments suggests a hitherto unappreciated role for Notch signaling in the regulation of autophagy.
source: The interaction between Notch and autophagy revealed in our experiments suggests a hitherto unappreciated role for Notch signaling in the regulation of this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Multiple studies have confirmed that the deficiency of Notch1 at later stages of T-cell development does not impair lineage commitment of Tregs.
source: Multiple studies have confirmed that the deficiency of Notch1 at later stages of T-cell development does not impair lineage commitment of Tregs.
evidence: This is a statement about published literature.

claim: Notch1 tunes a late event in the differentiation of Tregs already committed to the suppressor lineage.
source: We propose however, that Notch1 tunes a late event in the differentiation of Tregs already committed to the suppressor lineage.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Low-levels of immune challenge elicit features of inflammation in Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mice compared to Cre negative littermates.
source: This is consistent with our observation that low-levels of immune challenge elicit features of inflammation as compared to the Cre negative littermates.
evidence: This is an observation from the mouse phenotype analysis.

claim: Notch is implicated in instructive fate choices in the T-cell lineage, with commitment to T-cell fate the earliest amongst these.
source: Notch is implicated in instructive fate choices in the T-cell lineage, with commitment to T-cell fate the earliest amongst these (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Non-nuclear Notch1 activity is a critical determinant of Treg function as evidenced in assays of adoptive transfers.
source: Here we demonstrate a critical role for non-nuclear Notch1 activity, wherein Notch-autophagy interactions follow from immune stimulation and are important determinants of Treg function as evidenced in assays of adoptive transfers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Mice with an ablation of Notch1 in mature CD4+T-cells did not present overt inflammatory phenotypes.
source: Despite defects in Notch1-/-Treg function, mice with an ablation of Notch1 in mature CD4+T-cells did not present overt inflammatory phenotypes, which likely reflect its role in tuning responses of effector T-cells (Laky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the Cd4-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mouse analysis.

claim: The targeted deletion of Notch1 in the Treg lineage resulted in inflammatory features suggesting an integral role for Notch1 in Treg homeostasis.
source: However, the targeted deletion of Notch1 in the Treg lineage resulted in inflammatory features suggested an integral role for Notch1 in Treg homeostasis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Foxp3-Cre::Notch1lox/lox mouse phenotype.

claim: Notch1 activity in Tregs may be critical in specific contexts and redundant or non-essential in others.
source: The possibility that Notch1 activity in Tregs is critical in specific contexts and redundant or non-essential in others cannot be excluded (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation.

claim: The integration of autophagy and non-nuclear Notch activity may be a conserved mechanism that tunes cell-fate decisions governed by the receptor in other cell types.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the integration of autophagy and non-nuclear Notch activity may be a conserved mechanism that tunes cell-fate decisions governed by the receptor in other cell types.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.
